beats.text: A word processor does three things at once. It shows your text, reads your keys, and checks your spelling.
It does not need three processes. One process runs three threads.
A thread is a path of execution inside a process.
The threads share the process's code, its data, its heap, and its open files.
But each thread has its own program counter, its own registers, and its own stack.
So threads are cheap to create and to switch, they share data for free, and the screen stays responsive while another thread works.
In C, pthread create starts a new thread running a function. pthread join waits for it to finish.
Concurrency and parallelism sound alike. They are not.
On one core, threads take turns. Each makes progress, but only one runs at any instant. That is concurrency.
With two cores, two threads really run at the same moment. That is parallelism.
So more cores means more speed? Only for the part that can be split.
Say a quarter of the job must run serially. With two cores, the other three quarters are shared. The time drops to zero point six two five. A speedup of one point six.
Add cores forever, and the parallel part shrinks towards nothing. The serial quarter stays. The speedup can never pass one over S. Here, four.
User threads are managed by a library. Kernel threads are what the OS schedules.
Many to one: all user threads share one kernel thread. If one blocks, they all stop.
One to one: each user thread gets its own kernel thread. Linux and Windows do this.
Many to many: user threads share a sufficient number of kernel threads.
Sharing has a price. counter plus plus looks like one step. It is three: load, add, store.
Two threads both load zero. Both add one. Both store one. It should be two.
One update is lost. That is a race condition, and chapter six fixes it.
